RainCheck

Every weather app tells you what one provider thinks. RainCheck asks several, notices when one of them is wrong, and tells you what the rest agree on.

  • Kotlin
  • Android
  • Retrofit
  • WorkManager
  • AlarmManager
View source on GitHub

What It Does

A native Android weather app built on the classic View system rather than Compose. Current conditions, hourly and daily forecasts, severe weather alerts, and a notification system I actually leave switched on.

What makes it different is underneath. Forecast providers disagree, sometimes badly, and picking one means inheriting whatever that provider gets wrong in your area. RainCheck queries several and combines them, which turns a data-source problem into a statistics problem.

Key Features

  • Multi-source forecasts. Several providers are queried in parallel and reconciled into one number, so a single bad source can't skew what you see.
  • Three independent notification systems. A daily summary on an exact alarm, precipitation warnings on background work scheduling, and severe weather alerts from the national service. They're genuinely separate because their timing requirements are.
  • Shared notification plumbing. All three build content through one builder and check one event tracker for deduplication, so you don't get told about the same storm twice.
  • Precipitation classified properly. Rain, drizzle, thunderstorms, snow, and freezing rain or sleet are distinguished, each with its own notification wording. “Precipitation expected” isn't useful when the answer is black ice.
  • A real permission model. Location permission is treated as three states — always, while in use, and denied — rather than the usual granted/not-granted binary, because background notifications need something foreground display doesn't.
  • Considered motion. Theme switching animates, and screen transitions are set at theme level so navigation feels consistent everywhere.

How It Works

Combining sources that disagree

Averaging several forecasts sounds like a one-liner, and it isn't. A plain mean is exactly as vulnerable to one bad source as using that source alone — a provider reporting a temperature twenty degrees off drags the average with it, and the user has no way to know.

So before anything is averaged, outliers are rejected using a modified Z-score based on median absolute deviation. That's a robust measure: unlike standard deviation, it isn't itself distorted by the outlier it's meant to catch. Values too far from the median get dropped, and only the survivors are averaged. The result degrades gracefully — a provider going down or going haywire doesn't show a wrong number, it just widens the spread of what's left.

Disabled controls that explain themselves

If you haven't granted background location, the controls depending on it should look unavailable — but a fully disabled control can't tell you why, which leaves users stuck. The fix was separating the two concerns that “disabled” normally bundles: transparency handles the visual dimming so the control reads as inactive, while the touch handler stays live and shows an explanation with a route to fixing it.

An expand animation without the flash

Expanding a forecast row with Android's default automatic transition produced a visible flash, because the default runs its fade and its bounds change in sequence, briefly showing content at the wrong size. Composing the transition by hand, with bounds and fade running in parallel, removed it. Nobody notices this fix, which is the point.

A master switch that doesn't destroy your settings

Turning notifications off globally and back on used to reset every sub-setting to its default, silently undoing configuration the user had done deliberately. The master toggle now gates delivery without writing to the individual settings at all.

Published properly

The repository ships with a README, an architecture document, an API reference, a changelog and an MIT license. All traffic is HTTPS; the cleartext exemption was removed rather than left in “just in case”. Before release I removed dead utility classes, unused endpoints, stale manifest entries, orphaned strings and around 130 unused drawable icons, and renamed internals that had drifted from what they meant. A codebase that lies about itself is one you can't trust six months later.
